chapter: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
title: Being told he was adopted, strict upbringing, church choir, family support for music
summary: He says he was told he was adopted, was raised strictly, sang baritone in church, and that his family and relatives encouraged his music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Now, were your grandparents in Englewood or where were they?

No, like I said, I was the only kid, and as far as I know, I never will today quite remember whether it was true or not, but I was told that I was an adopted kid, you know. Of course, it makes no difference to me, you know. And, of course --
You were told by whom, by your parents or by somebody outside the family?

Outside, which come to think of it, I probably was because by my birth certificate I was under a different name, come to think of it, but that didn't make a difference. As far as my parents were concerned, that was the real thing for me, you know. They raised me. I will never forget and appreciate the way they raised me. They really had -- you might say they made something out of me, you know, helped me to make something out of myself, you know.
Now, you say you had a very disciplined, very strict kind of --
Very strict, yes, right.
You learned that, like you had chores you were supposed to do?
The chores and, of course, I -- they didn't have to make me, but I was used to going to church, you know, and I sang in the choir. And I did.
What did you say you sang? You sang alto?
No, I sang baritone-like.
Oh, you sang baritone? That's funny because from hearing you sing with the bass, I would have thought you sang alto.

No. With the bass it's a different octave above when I'm playing thing, especially when I'm singing and (inaudible) the bow, which I'd like to get into the reason why I got into this, on account of --
The violin.
-- the violin, the violin's sight -Ray Perry. And we happened to be working in the same group, Dean Earl --
Right.
-- his orchestra. And we played in this nightclub, and the Little Dixie, it was called. And that's where I got the idea to hum along with my bass fiddle.
Now, when you were -- getting back to --

I'm trying to get some -- fill in a few things, as much background, early, as -- you didn't have, when your family became aware of the fact that you were going to become a musician, were -- they didn't try to discourage you or anything?
No, they didn't. In fact, they encouraged me. And that's like when I wanted to go away to study, they were all for it, you know. And that's how I wound up in -- at the Conservatory in Boston.
Now, did you -- did you meet other wings of your family other than your mother and father? Were any of them musically inclined or --
No. Come to think of it, none of them -- my so called cousins, what have you, uncle, what have you.
None of them were musicians?
No, only one.
Did they all live in New Jersey?
Yeah.
So you didn't have any -- you didn't have any -- did you ever have any contact with any members of your family in the South or Midwest or anything like that?
No.
No, it was all there?
Right there in Englewood, yes.
Englewood of thereabouts?
Thereabouts, yes.
